source.title: Identity prediction errors in the human midbrain update reward-identity expectations in the orbitofrontal cortex.

confidence_rationale: Human fMRI with a value-matched transreinforcer reversal design that isolates outcome IDENTITY from value; OFC encodes reward-identity expectations updated by midbrain identity prediction errors. Directly supports MECH-346's core premise that the goal seed is an object-identity representation, not a value scalar. Docked for BOLD-level (not single-cell) resolution and appetitive-odor task vs REE gridworld objects.
failure_signatures: Identity and value error signals in the midbrain are correlated and share a common neural origin, so an identity-only seed that ignores value covariation may be biologically incomplete.
Demonstrated for appetitive food-odor outcomes only; whether identity expectations seed a prospective goal latent for spatial/foraging objects is untested here.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Identity-based prediction errors in the human midbrain support the formation of outcome-identity expectations in OFC, dissociable from value.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-346 seeds z_goal from the most-wanted object's z_object (an identity-bearing latent) rather than a raw scalar z_resource snapshot; the paper grounds the claim that the brain maintains a distinct outcome-IDENTITY representation that can drive goal expectation independent of cached value.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The paper measures fMRI BOLD identity-expectation signals in OFC; it does not demonstrate that an identity representation is used as a generative SEED for a prospective goal/policy latent. The REE mechanism's 'most-wanted' selection over per-axis drive is an additional step the paper does not test.
mapping.source_context: Human fMRI (n=adults), transreinforcer reversal learning with value-matched appetitive food odors.

confidence_components.notes: High-quality human evidence with a clean identity-vs-value dissociation; main risk is the seed-vs-readout distinction and species/task transfer.
